newsitem.title: UK: N. Irish politician Hume denies presidency bid.
newsitem.headline: N. Irish politician Hume denies presidency bid.

text.p: John Hume, a moderate Irish nationalist leader and an architect of the Northern Ireland peace process, on Friday denied reports he might seek the Irish presidency.
"There is absolutely no truth in the reports," said Hume, a member of the British parliament and leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP).
He issued a statement dismissing the suggestion as the "product of silly season journalism".

Speculation that Hume might stand as a candidate for president of Ireland arose after he declined to say in a radio interview on Thursday whether he would stand in his Foyle constituency in Londonderry in the next British parliamentary election, due by next May.

The Guardian newspaper said Hume could stand for the Irish presidency if current head of state Mary Robinson decided not to seek a second term from November. Her decision is likely within the next few weeks.
Under the Irish constitution, anyone in the British province of Northern Ireland has the right to be regarded as an Irish citizen and therefore to stand for the presidency.
However, Hume's future as a British member of parliament is still unclear.
Joe Hendron, an SDLP member of parliament, said Hume had not decided whether to stand again for parliament.
"He has the massive role, not only of leader of the SDLP, but also as a member of the European Parliament. He has not made up his mind yet as to whether he will run," Hendron told Irish radio.
The Guardian said Robinson had lent weight to the previously symbolic role of the president.
"As a consequence, the suitability of the position as a vehicle for promoting the peace process might appeal to Mr Hume, whose popularity with Irish voters is constant," it said.

Hume has been a prime mover in the drive to find a political solution to the conflict in Northern Ireland. Irish Republican Army guerrillas, fighting against British rule of the province, ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.

The Guardian said there were concerns within the SDLP that Hume's seat could fall to Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, if Hume did not stand. That would boost Sinn Fein's efforts to become the main Irish nationalist party in Northern Ireland.
